item.title: How ASEAN Responded to the ICJ’s Myanmar Genocide Ruling
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Last week’s landmark ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) is likely to have unpredictable political and diplomatic ramifications for the architecture of international criminal justice in general and Myanmar in particular.

By a vote of nine to six, the ICJ ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims during a military “clearance operation” in northern Rakhine State in 2017. During the operation, it found that Myanmar’s security forces “killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence as well as acts of extreme violence against children and attacked fleeing Rohingya as they sought to flee in large numbers to Bangladesh.”

The court ordered Myanmar to provide reparations to victims and allow the “safe and dignified return to their place of residence and the reunification of families for the Rohingya displaced as a result of Myanmar’s wrongful acts.” Judges also said it should take measures to prevent further violations of the Genocide Convention.

Enforcing the judgment on Myanmar, which has since rejected the ICJ’s determination as “unfair” and a “great disappointment,” is likely to be challenging, and will depend on whether foreign governments can muster the political will.

Many Western governments have expressed their support for the ruling, the most outspoken of which has been the United Kingdom. Foreign Secretary David Miliband said in a statement that the U.K. “reaffirms our full support for the Court and the international legal order, and condemns the horrific treatment of the Rohingya people by the Myanmar military regime.” Stating that it was “determined to act and ensure accountability for these appalling crimes,” Miliband said that his government had ordered the expulsion of the Myanmar defense attaché from the U.K. and called “urgently” for a U.N. Security Council session to discuss the judgment.

Other Western powers such as Australia, Norway, and the European Union have issued similar statements, as has the United States, albeit in a more restrained key.

In comparison, the response from Southeast Asia has been decidedly muted. As of press time, only two ASEAN governments – the Philippines and Malaysia – had issued official statements about the ruling, and only one other – Thailand – had addressed it at length. Brunei, Cambodia, Vietnam, Laos, Timor-Leste, Vietnam, and Indonesia have so far not responded to the judgment.

The most supportive statement came from Malaysia, whose Foreign Ministry said yesterday that it “respects” the ICJ’s ruling, and that it would engage with the United Nations, ASEAN, and the Organization of Islamic Cooperation, on whose behalf The Gambia brought the case against Myanmar in 2019, “on matters arising from the judgment.”

“Malaysia reaffirms its commitment to upholding international law, including its responsibilities as a State Party to the Genocide Convention,” the Ministry said. It added that Malaysia would “continue to advocate for a comprehensive and durable resolution to this protracted crisis.”

There are a number of possible reasons for Malaysia’s supportive position. Kuala Lumpur has been perhaps the ASEAN member state most critical of Myanmar since the military coup of 2021. However, it has recently begun to moderate its position, and last month, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim hosted coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing with full state honors. The ostensible reason for this was to facilitate the return of refugees and asylum seekers to Myanmar, amid a recent rise in hate speech and anti-Rohingya sentiment that has put political pressure on Anwar’s government.

Malaysia’s relatively supportive position on the ICJ ruling may also have something to do with the possible application of the precedent of the Myanmar case to Israel. In 2024, South Africa brought a case against Israel, accusing it of committing genocide against the Palestinians of Gaza, and much of the international response to The Gambia vs. Myanmar judgment has concerned its possible implications for this case. Prime Minister Anwar is a long-time critic of Israel and has been the most outspoken ASEAN leader on Israel’s actions in Gaza since October 2023, an issue that also reflects a strong domestic political consensus in Malaysia. It is plausible that Malaysia’s supportive stance is less a reflection of its attitude toward Myanmar and more an indication of how the ICJ may soon rule on the Israel-Palestine issue.

The Philippines’ reaction to the ICJ ruling was slightly more ambiguous. The country’s Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) stated that it “acknowledges” the judgment and “reaffirms its support for the peaceful settlement of disputes and full adherence to international law, including the obligations of States under the Genocide Convention.” It added, “The Philippines likewise underscores the importance of respecting the decisions of the International Court of Justice as the principal judicial organ of the United Nations.” The DFA also reiterated its “deep concern” about the humanitarian consequences of conflict, particularly for civilians and other vulnerable populations.

Thailand did not issue an official statement, but Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said over the weekend that it will maintain relations with Myanmar despite the ICJ ruling. Anutin’s administration has been a strong advocate of a policy of “calibrated engagement” with Myanmar since a quasi-civilian administration took office in April, a position that ASEAN as a whole adopted at this month’s summit.

Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow on Friday described the ICJ judgment as a legal matter between Myanmar and the ICJ that would not derail Bangkok’s engagement with Naypyidaw, which he said was consistent with ASEAN’s consensus.…

Source: The Diplomat | Published: 2026-11-23 02:16 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Mongolia’s Foreign Policy Doctrine and the ‘Third Neighbor’
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: original reporting, historical context

Mongolia’s fundamental foreign policy doctrine is to develop balanced relations with its two neighbors, China and Russia, while cultivating ties with a “Third Neighbor,” without becoming overly dependent on either bordering state. For a country whose only neighbors are China and Russia, the “Third Neighbor” concept is also a strategy for national survival.

The concept was given formal shape in the “Concept of Foreign Policy of Mongolia,” adopted by the Parliament of Mongolia on June 30, 1994. It set as the highest priority the development of balanced, good-neighborly relations with both Russia and China without excessive dependence on either, and then the expansion of relations with advanced democracies. In a February 10, 2011 revision, the “Third Neighbor” was explicitly named, and the concept was broadened to include not only advanced democracies but also countries such as India, South Korea, and Turkey.

The impetus for that revision was Mongolia’s rapidly growing economic dependence on China, which had made it impossible to maintain balance between China and Russia. The revision aimed to limit over-reliance on China and to more actively promote security and economic cooperation with Third Neighbor countries as a counterweight. At the root of the Third Neighbor policy, therefore, lies wariness of China.

Wedged between China and Russia, that wariness toward China has strong roots in Mongolian public sentiment, a reflection of the country’s historical experience. Since its Declaration of Independence in 1911, Mongolia has repeatedly faced existential crises, most of which originated from the Republic of China (ROC) or the People’s Republic of China (PRC) to the south.

The Qing Dynasty, which held sway over most of East Asia from the seventeenth century, was a pre-modern empire that integrated a Manchu imperial house with Mongol nobility, Han bureaucrats, and Tibetan Buddhist authorities. When the Xinhai Revolution broke out on October 10, 1911, however, the dynasty’s hold began to crumble rapidly. The princes and lamas of Outer Mongolia (present-day Mongolia) decided to break from the Qing, declaring independence on December 1, 1911, and on December 29 enthroning Bogd Gegeen VIII, the supreme leader of Tibetan Buddhism, as Bogd Khan (Emperor) and establishing the Bogd Khan government. The Qing Dynasty itself was formally dissolved on February 12, 1912, when Puyi, the Xuantong Emperor, abdicated.

The newly established ROC, however, refused to recognize Mongolian independence, claiming to be “the successor to all territories of the Qing Dynasty.” Under the 1915 Kyakhta Treaty, a compromise was reached among Russia, China, and Mongolia: Outer Mongolia would acknowledge Chinese suzerainty in exchange for retaining autonomy. That arrangement was shattered in 1919 when Chinese warlord Xu Shuzheng invaded Outer Mongolia in breach of the agreement and abolished its autonomy.

In the face of this crisis, revolutionaries led by Damdin Sükhbaatar launched a movement to restore independence. In early 1921, Baron Ungern of the Russian White Army drove out the Chinese forces. By July of that year, however, the Mongolian People’s Army, backed by the Soviet Russian Red Army, had seized the capital and established a People’s Government. The Bogd Khan was left as a nominal head of state, but real power had passed to the revolutionary government.

When the Bogd Khan died in May 1924, the revolutionary government declined to restore the monarchy, declaring the establishment of the Mongolian People’s Republic on November 26 of that year. Mongolia thus set out from the independence movement of 1911, shaped by the threat from China and the influence of the Russian Revolution, to emerge in 1924 as a modern state with a socialist orientation, now firmly under Soviet influence.

The ROC recognized Mongolian independence in 1946, only to rescind that recognition in 1953; exchanges between the two countries did not begin until 2002. The PRC established diplomatic relations with Mongolia on October 16, 1949, shortly after its own founding. Even before that, however, Mao Zedong had approached the Soviet Union about placing Mongolia under Chinese control. Mao would occasionally reveal ambitions for Mongolian annexation in later years.

Given China’s historical refusal to recognize the independence of Outer Mongolia, Mongolia viewed Mao’s intentions with deep alarm. As the Sino-Soviet dispute, which began in the late 1950s, escalated into full confrontation in the 1960s, Mongolia, feeling acutely threatened, concluded the Treaty of Friendship, Cooperation and Mutual Assistance with the Soviet Union in 1966, deepening its reliance on the Soviet alliance.

During the Cultural Revolution of the late 1960s, China denounced Mongolia as “revisionist,” and persecution of ethnic Mongolians occurred in Inner Mongolia — developments that made Mongolia acutely conscious of a military threat from China. As the Sino-Soviet border conflict intensified, the Soviet Union stationed large-scale forces inside Mongolia.

Mongolia’s predicament in this period was that, while it preserved its independence by depending on the Soviet Union for security, excessive dependence on Moscow had cost it diplomatic autonomy. Proposals for Soviet annexation of Mongolia even circulated during the Brezhnev era. Mongolia resisted, but in practical terms it was treated as though it were a Soviet constituent republic.

In the late 1980s, Gorbachev’s moves to improve Sino-Soviet relations brought the Sino-Soviet split toward resolution, and Soviet troops began withdrawing from Mongolia. Through the democratic revolution of 1990 and the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991, followed by the adoption of a new constitution and the country’s renaming as Mongolia in 1992, Mongolia finally shed its total dependence on the Soviet Union.…

item.title: Diplomacy or Transparency? Philippine Officials Consider Approach Amid Rising China Tension
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, political analysis

Philippine Foreign Affairs Secretary Ma. Theresa Lazaro announced on the last day of the 49th Summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) that provisional agreements have been reached with China on more than 80 percent of the text of the region’s draft Code of Conduct in the South China Sea, or COC. This means the Philippines ended its ASEAN chairmanship without finalizing the COC, which was designed to peacefully handle maritime differences.

But Lazaro was not just presiding over the COC negotiations and assisting President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. in overseeing the ASEAN summit preparations. She also had to contend with serious criticisms about her work.

No less than the country’s ombudsman accused the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) of turning visa issuance in China into a business. The DFA denied this and called out the ombudsman for undermining its institutional integrity and maligning the reputation of foreign service personnel.

Meanwhile, human rights groups strongly denounced Lazaro’s recent high-profile visit to Myanmar to distribute aid in cooperation with junta-appointed agencies, and called it a legitimization of war criminals under the guise of humanitarian diplomacy.

But it was the escalatory war of words between some Philippine defense officials and the Chinese embassy in Manila over maritime disputes that grabbed headlines for weeks and forced Lazaro to intervene several times and remind Chinese diplomats not to erode mutual trust and confidence between the two countries.

The tension worsened to the point that it alarmed business and sectoral groups which released a public statement calling for de-escalation and the avoidance of “inflammatory rhetoric” that could further strain bilateral relations, including the promotion and protection of livelihoods and stable economic exchanges.

The DFA publicly endorsed the call and issued a separate statement about the “essence of statecraft,” and the supremacy of diplomacy in dealing with matters involving other countries. It did not mention names or offices, but the statement was clearly referring to defense officials who have been actively denouncing China’s narratives and actions related to the West Philippine Sea.

It asserted that civilian authorities should direct the country’s international relations and the importance of having a united stand. “In high-stakes diplomacy, a disciplined and coherent national voice remains essential to advancing our national interests,” it stated.

It highlighted that transparency is a tool but one that cannot substitute for strategy or statecraft. And it made sure that this point was clearly directed at the Philippine Coast Guard and other defense officials who have been regularly providing the public and the world with video evidence of China’s illegal activities in the country’s maritime territories.

“Releasing footage or shaping an online narrative does not, by itself, act as a physical deterrent at sea or a legal strategy,” the DFA said.

It added that the 2016 South China Sea Arbitral Award “was secured through rigorous legal proceedings under international law, not through public messaging or social media.”

It is mainly through diplomacy that the country negotiates disputes and formal protests. The DFA clarified that diplomatic engagement is not appeasement. “There are moments when public disclosure serves strategic purposes, and moments when discretion, restraint, and quiet engagement produce better results,” the DFA emphasized.

No defense official contradicted the DFA statement. But some political parties questioned why the DFA is reprimanding officials who have been exposing China’s illegal actions and harassment of fisherfolk. They expressed concern that aside from directing everyone to censor their views on the issue, the DFA’s stance appears to serve the interests of Beijing.

President Marcos’ spokesperson supported the DFA statement and called for unity ahead of the ASEAN Summit. At the same time, the official acknowledged that the statements and actions of defense officials are in line with their official duties.

What the DFA statement revealed was the internal differences in the Cabinet on adopting the best approach in addressing the rising tension with China. The country’s hosting duties for the ASEAN summit provided the DFA with the opportunity to aggressively put forward its views on the matter and receive the president’s backing.

Now that the summit has ended and the facilitation of the COC negotiations has been handed over to another ASEAN member state (Singapore), will the DFA retain the lead in promoting government discourse on issues involving China and the West Philippine Sea? Or will defense officials resume their active media engagement on China’s provocative maritime buildup and the necessity of strengthening military alliances, mainly with the United States and its allies, to serve as a deterrent?

If it finds itself sidelined by competing factions, the DFA should enjoin stakeholders to build a broader consensus on the value of making diplomacy work at all costs. More importantly, a citizen-led movement should amplify the call about what it really means to pursue an independent foreign policy.

Source: The Diplomat | Published: 2026-11-23 01:33 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

Original link: https://thediplomat.com/2026/11/diplomacy-or-transparency-philippine-officials-consider-approach-amid-rising-china-tension/

item.title: UK taxpayers held more than £1tn in offshore tax havens, latest HMRC data shows
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, financial analysis

The amount of money UK taxpayers hold in offshore accounts in tax havens has exceeded £1tn for the first time, raising concerns about potential losses to the public purse.

HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) data, obtained by the TaxWatch thinktank through freedom of information requests, shows between 2022 and 2024 the value of balances held offshore in tax havens increased by 10%. These were the latest available figures.

The list of tax havens represented in the HMRC data was based on one originally put together by academics from the EU Tax Observatory, and includes jurisdictions such as Hong Kong, the Isle of Jersey, Switzerland, Liechtenstein and Panama.

While much of the money in the offshore accounts will have been correctly declared to the UK’s tax authority, large sums are still proving hard to track down and claw back.

HMRC managed to secure an average of £125m in previously unpaid tax, interest on penalties, from offshore accounts – including those held in tax havens – each year, according to the data provided to TaxWatch.

That is thanks to information shared through agreements such as the common reporting standard (CRS), which commits countries to exchange information about foreigners’ bank accounts, as part of efforts to crack down on tax evasion and fraud.

However, HMRC previously estimated that £200m to £700m was going unpaid across all offshore accounts on average each year, according to a 2018 snapshot it provided.

And TaxWatch said about a fifth of offshore accounts owned by UK taxpayers were declared through the CRS system without a unique taxpayer identifier, which are meant to be gathered by the banks or financial firms that hold the accounts. That makes it difficult for HMRC to match undeclared accounts with individual taxpayers.

That has raised concerns about how much potential UK tax revenue may be disappearing via accounts held in tax havens, such as the British Virgin Islands and Bermuda, which are known for their low taxes and corporate secrecy.

HMRC announced plans to clamp down on wealthy taxpayers recently, including those who may be storing assets overseas.

That has involved assigning dedicated “customer compliance managers” to more than 200 billionaires, to help tackle a “wealthy tax gap” caused by those who do not pay what they should. HMRC estimates it could end up raising at least £500m towards a larger commitment to secure £10bn of additional tax revenues by 2030.

HMRC was grilled in July last year by MPs on the parliamentary public accounts committee over its lack of understanding of tax compliance by about 1.3 million wealthy taxpayers.

Mike Lewis, the director of TaxWatch, said: “Last month’s budget brought the welcome announcement of a new HMRC plan to increase wealthy and offshore tax compliance. These new figures show that plan will require more resources, expertise and time.

“Much less unpaid tax is being recovered from offshore accounts than HMRC’s estimate of tax evasion in such accounts – an estimate which only covers accounts automatically notified to HMRC, and which UK taxpayers hold in their own names.

“That’s the lowest-hanging fruit. Most tax evasion happens behind much more complex structures.”

TaxWatch said HMRC had repeatedly postponed publishing estimates of all the tax going unpaid on offshore income and gains, leaving the public and government unable to properly benchmark the tax authority’s effectiveness in tackling offshore tax evasion and non-compliance.

An HMRC spokesperson said: “We’ve led the way in increasing global tax transparency, helping us tackle offshore tax risks and ensure everyone pays the right amount under UK law.

“We’ve already strengthened our approach by bringing together specialist expertise to take on the most complex offshore risks, and we’re deploying an additional 400 people to tackle wealthy offshore non-compliance by 2030.”

Source: The Guardian Politics | Published: 2026-11-22 15:43 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: Pip review will call for overhaul rather than scrapping benefit for under-25s
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: original reporting, policy analysis

A long-awaited review of the personal independence payment (Pip) system will this week recommend that it is overhauled, a week after another report called for it to be partly scrapped.

The final report on Pip by a committee co-led by Stephen Timms, the social security minister, is expected to be published as soon as Tuesday, presenting Andy Burnham with one of his most politically sensitive decisions yet as prime minister.

Its conclusions, shaped with the input of disability rights advocates, are understood to be very similar to a draft set of recommendations that emerged in September, which called for a series of changes, particularly to the system of assessment, to take better account of conditions that vary over time.

This would involve significant changes to Pip, which is intended to help disabled people meet the extra costs of disability. An interim report by Timms’ committee described the benefit as widely valued but “no longer fit for purpose”.

However, it would retain the system for all ages, while last week’s report by Alan Milburn on worklessness among young people called for it to be scrapped for adults under 25 and replaced by an “additional cost allowance”, part of a wider network of job-based help for this age group.

Government officials have pushed back on the idea of a clash, saying Milburn’s review was commissioned after the Timms process had begun, and that about 90% of the Pip caseload involves people over 25.

But with Timms’ recommendations understood to be quite broad, Burnham and his ministers will need to make a series of decisions about what comes next, on a deeply sensitive subject. Keir Starmer was forced to abandon planned changes in 2025 after a rebellion by Labour MPs.

There was widespread shock among disability campaigners and charities at the Milburn report’s recommendations to scrap Pip and universal credit health benefit payments for under-25s as part of efforts to boost jobs and training for young people not in education, employment or training.

The review steering group is co-chaired by Timms and the disability rights advocates Clenton Farquharson and Sharon Brennan, and most of its 12 members have lived experience of disability or long-term health conditions.

There are reportedly worries among some members of the Timms review board over the scale of Milburn’s proposals on Pip, which would cut £3.6bn from spending on young people. “Some members are really concerned,” one source told the Guardian.

The report will include short-term overhauls, within the current spending round, and longer-term ones. Many of the specifics for the latter would need to be decided by ministers before they legislate next year.

Burnham faces pressure from the Conservatives to reduce the overall cost of working-age benefits. He has said this is his plan but he has pushed back against the idea of what he called “crude cuts”, saying these often just created costs elsewhere.

The Timms review, framed by ministers as a groundbreaking “co-produced” policy initiative, was seen as an attempt to restore trust among disabled people after the collapse of the Pip plans under Starmer, which were based on £5bn in cuts.

The interim report in July and further emerging findings in September confirmed a consensus view that Pip was unfit for purpose and that a major overhaul was needed to make the benefit fair, humane and efficient.

It raised the prospect that some claimants could in future receive “in kind” awards such as services, aid or training alongside basic cash awards.

But it underlined that cash payments were “the foundation” of a future reformed disability benefit, that it would not be means-tested and that any “reformed benefit will be designed with disabled people and those with long-term health conditions, and tested to make sure it works before it is rolled out”. There was no mention of scrapping Pip for under-25s or any other age groups.

Until recently, most disability charities had been optimistic that the Timms review – the remit of which did not include the costs of Pip or potential cuts in spending – would lead to much-needed changes and improve the lives of the 4 million adults who claim it.

But the timing and scope of the Milburn review, which has been conspicuously welcomed by ministers, has dented that confidence.

A spokesperson for the Department for Work and Pensions said: “The Timms review interim report made clear that Pip is no longer fit for purpose. When the final report is published, we will consider the recommendations alongside the Milburn review.”

Source: The Guardian Politics | Published: 2026-11-22 17:32 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100
